5.title: Children of the Day
5.overview:
The final chapter of 1 Thessalonians divides naturally into three movements: the Day of the Lord (vv. 1–11), final instructions for community life (vv. 12–22), and the closing prayer and benediction (vv. 23–28). Together they complete the letter's arc: from the gospel received (chapter 1) through pastoral love and suffering (chapters 2–3) through holy living and resurrection hope (chapter 4) to eschatological identity and the sanctifying God who will complete what he has begun (chapter 5).

The great identity-declaration of this chapter is 'you are all children of light and children of the day' (v. 5). This is not an aspiration but a declaration — a statement of who they already are by virtue of the gospel they have received and the Spirit who indwells them. The ethical exhortations that follow (be sober, put on the breastplate of faith and love, encourage one another, pray without ceasing) are not ways of becoming children of the day. They are the life-pattern of those who already are. Identity precedes imperative. Grace precedes obedience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having answered what happens to the Christian dead, Paul answers the question that follows — when? — by declining it. About times and seasons they need nothing written (v.1), since they already know the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night (v.2). While people are saying 'peace and security', destruction arrives like labour pains, and there is no escaping it (v.3).

But they are not in darkness for that day to catch them out (v.4), because they are all children of light and of the day, belonging neither to night nor darkness (v.5). So they are not to sleep as others do but to keep awake and sober (v.6) — for sleeping and drunkenness are night activities (v.7), and since they belong to the day they are to be sober, wearing the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation (v.8).

The ground of it all: God has not appointed them for wrath but for obtaining salvation through the Lord Jesus (v.9), who died for them so that whether awake or asleep they will live with him (v.10). Therefore they are to encourage one another and build one another up, as they are already doing (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Destined for Wrath

Verse 9 answers a fear the letter has been raising since 1:10. The verb means to appoint beforehand — the same root as the 'appointed' of 3:3, where affliction was described as a posting. God's purpose for these people was settled in advance, and it was settled on salvation rather than wrath. The reason is not their performance but a substitution: 'through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us' — the only place in this letter where Paul states it that directly.

Note that 'obtain salvation' uses a word for acquisition, a coming-into-possession. Salvation is here spoken of as still ahead, something to be entered as an heir enters an estate. And the clause 'whether we are awake or asleep' deliberately reuses the vocabulary of 4:13-18: alive or dead when he comes, the outcome is identical. That is the real comfort — not that they will live to see it, which Paul never promises and none of them did, but that it will make no difference.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Peace and security' was close to an imperial slogan. The pax Romana was Rome's proudest claim, and Thessalonica — a free city that had backed Rome and prospered — had every reason to believe the advertising. Paul quotes the slogan and identifies it as the moment of collapse: a civilisation announcing its own permanence is the least prepared thing there is. His labour-pain image is exact in a way worth noticing — labour is sudden in onset but never unexpected, and once begun it cannot be called off.

Now: The thief image (from Jesus, Matt 24:43) is about unannouncement, not menace — which is why every attempt to calculate the date is not merely difficult but a contradiction of the teaching. And note the order of verses 5-6: 'you are children of light' comes before 'let us keep awake'. Paul never asks people to become something in order to qualify; he tells them what they are and asks them to live like it. Getting that order backwards is what produces exhausted Christians. The armour of verse 8 repays attention too — faith, love and hope, the triad of 1:3, handed back at the end as equipment, with hope as the helmet because a church losing its grip on the future stops thinking clearly about the present.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 4 answered the question they had asked: what about our dead? Chapter 5 answers the one they were bound to ask next: when?

And Paul's answer is a polite refusal. 'Concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you.' Two words: chronos, duration, clock time; and kairos, the decisive moment, the right occasion. Between them they cover every form the question can take — how long, and at what point. Paul declines both.

He is almost certainly echoing his Lord. When the disciples asked whether the kingdom was being restored at that time, Jesus answered: it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7) — the same pair of words. Paul had evidently been taught that answer and passed it on.

Note the striking implication of 'you have no need.' They already knew what they needed to know, and Paul had told them in a stay of a few weeks. What they had been taught was not a schedule but a certainty and a posture.

'The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.' The phrase 'the day of the LORD' comes from the prophets, where it is the day God settles accounts — darkness and not light, as Amos says to people who were looking forward to it (Amos 5:18-20). Paul hands the Old Testament's name for God's own day of reckoning to Jesus without a word of explanation.

And the thief image comes from Jesus himself (Matt 24:43). Notice what it does and does not say. A thief is not dangerous because he is malicious but because he does not send word. The image is about unannouncement, not menace — which is exactly why calculating the date is not merely difficult but a contradiction of the teaching. Every generation that has produced a timetable has been wrong, and was refuted by this sentence before it began.

verseByVerse.quote: While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'While people are saying, "There is peace and security."' Those two words together — eirene kai asphaleia — were very close to a Roman slogan. The pax Romana was the empire's proudest claim and its central promise: peace, and safety, guaranteed by the legions. Coins and inscriptions said so. Thessalonica, a free city that had backed Rome and prospered for it, had every reason to believe the advertising.

Paul quotes the slogan and says it is precisely the moment of collapse. Not that the empire is wicked, but that a civilisation announcing its own permanence is the least prepared thing there is. The words are not a warning sign of danger; they are the danger.

'Then sudden destruction will come upon them as labour pains come upon a pregnant woman.' The image repays a moment, because it is not simply a picture of pain.

Labour is sudden in its onset — no one is told the hour. But it is not unexpected: the woman has known for months that it is coming, and it does not arrive out of nowhere. That is the exact combination Paul wants. The day is unpredictable in timing and entirely predictable in fact. Anyone claiming to be taken by surprise had the information all along.

And once it starts it cannot be called off. 'They will not escape.' The word is used of fleeing successfully, getting clear. Labour is the one process no one talks their way out of; it has to be gone through.

One thing more should be said, because the image is not only severe. What labour ends in is a birth. The New Testament uses birth-pain language for the end of the age precisely because the pains are not the point — they are what precedes something being born. Paul does not develop it here; he is writing about those who are caught out. But the picture he chose carries a future the slogan never had.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But you' — and the whole paragraph turns. Everything to this point has been about 'them', the people saying peace and security. Now Paul addresses the church, and what he says is not that they will avoid the day but that it will not surprise them.

'You are not in darkness, for that day to surprise you like a thief.' The thief is a problem for the household that is asleep. For a house with its lights on and someone awake, the arrival is not a catastrophe. The difference is not in the thief's timing; it is in who is awake.

Then the identity, and it comes before any command: 'you are all children of light, children of the day.' The Hebrew idiom 'son of' means belonging to, characterised by — sons of light are people whose nature is light. Paul is not telling them to become something. He is telling them what they are.

Do not miss the little word all. Not the mature ones or the leaders. Every believer in that congregation, including the fainthearted and the weak he will name in verse 14, is a child of the day.

And notice the pronoun shifting under him. 'You are all children of light' — then, immediately, 'we are not of the night or of the darkness.' Paul cannot keep himself out of it. He is not a teacher describing a class of people; he is one of them.

This is the order Paul's ethics always follow, and getting it backwards produces exhausted Christians. He does not say: stay awake, and then you will be children of light. He says: you are children of light — therefore stay awake. The command in the next verse rests on a fact already true, and that is the difference between being asked to become something and being asked to live like what you are.

verseByVerse.quote: So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So then' — here is the conclusion drawn from the identity. Three imperatives, and the first is negative: 'let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.'

The sleep here is not the sleep of 4:13-15, where it was a tender word for the Christian dead. Paul has changed its use deliberately within a page. Here it is moral insensibility — the drowsiness of a person who has stopped paying attention. And note 'let us': Paul includes himself in the warning. He does not consider himself immune from spiritual drowsiness.

Two positive commands answer it. Keep awake — the word for staying alert, used of the watchman and of the disciples in Gethsemane, who failed at it. And be sober — nepho, the opposite of intoxicated: clear-headed, in possession of your judgement, able to see what is actually there.

Sobriety is the underrated Christian virtue, and it repays a pause on what it means here. It is not solemnity — this letter commands rejoicing ten verses later. It is the capacity to assess things accurately: to know what is temporary and what is permanent, and not to be talked into a false estimate of either. Drunkenness is the standing biblical picture of misjudgement, of a man who thinks he is fine and is not.

Then verse 7, which the older text lost, and which supplies Paul's reasoning: 'those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night.' It is an observation about ordinary life in the ancient city, where the night belonged to sleeping and to carousing, and the day to work.

The argument is one of fitness. Sleeping and drunkenness are night activities — they belong to the dark. And these people, he has just said, do not belong to the night at all. So moral drowsiness in a Christian is not merely dangerous; it is out of place, like a man asleep in the street at noon. Paul is not threatening them into wakefulness. He is pointing out that they are dressed for the wrong hour.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the verse that vanished from the older text, and it is the practical heart of the paragraph — because Paul now says how a person actually stays awake.

'Since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.' Sobriety is not achieved by trying harder to concentrate. It is achieved by getting dressed.

The picture is a soldier, and Paul is drawing on Isaiah, where the LORD himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation on his head (Isa 59:17). What God wears, his people are given to wear. Paul will develop the same image at length in Ephesians 6.

And notice what the armour is made of: faith, love and hope. The triad from the very first paragraph of the letter (1:3) comes back at the end as equipment. What Paul thanked God for in chapter 1 he now hands them as protection — the same three things, first as evidence of God's work, now as the means of survival.

The placement matters too. Faith and love cover the chest, over the heart and lungs — what keeps you alive. Hope is the helmet, over the head — what keeps you thinking straight. That is exactly right for this letter. A church losing its grip on the future does not merely become sad; it becomes unable to think clearly about the present, which is what had happened when their friends died. Hope is not decoration. It is what protects your judgement.

And observe that this armour is entirely defensive. There is no sword here. Paul is not arming them for a campaign; he is equipping them to stay upright until the day comes. That is the whole ambition of the paragraph: be awake, be sober, still standing.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the ground under everything, and it answers the fear that the wrath language has been raising since 1:10: 'God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.'

The verb means to appoint, to set in place beforehand — the same root as the 'appointed' of 3:3, where affliction was a posting. Paul is speaking of God's purpose settled in advance. And the point is what it is settled on: not wrath. Whatever the day of the Lord means for the world, it does not mean that for these people, and the reason is not their performance.

Note also 'to obtain salvation'. The word means acquisition, a possessing. Salvation here is still ahead of them — something to be come into, as an heir comes into an estate. Paul can speak of salvation as past, present and future, and here it is the future he needs: they are not hoping to be spared, they are on their way to collect.

'Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us.' There is the mechanism, and it is the only place in this letter where Paul states the substitution directly. Why are they not destined for wrath? Not because God overlooks things. Because someone else stood where they were standing.

Then the clause that ties the two chapters together: 'so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him.' He is reaching back to 4:13-18 and using the same vocabulary — awake meaning alive, asleep meaning dead. The Thessalonians had been frightened that the dead would be at a disadvantage. Paul says the death of Jesus settled that too: alive or dead when he comes, the outcome is identical.

And that is the real comfort of the passage. Not that they will be alive at the parousia — Paul does not know and does not promise it, and in fact every one of them died. The promise is that it will not matter. 'We might live with him' is the same note that ended chapter 4: always with the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.'

It is the second time in two paragraphs that Paul has ended a passage about the last day with an instruction to talk to each other (4:18). That is his settled view of what this teaching is for. Eschatology in the New Testament is not given to satisfy curiosity or to sort Christians into camps; it is given to be used on people who need it.

'Build one another up' is oikodomeo, the word for constructing a building — the same root as the edifice, and behind our word edify. It implies something being raised course by course, and it implies a plan. Encouragement in the New Testament is not generalised niceness; it is structural work on another person, adding to what is already standing.

Note again who does it. Not Paul, and not the leaders he is about to mention in verse 12. 'One another' — the ordinary members of a congregation, doing to each other what he has just done to them in two chapters of teaching. This assumes believers who know enough doctrine to have something to say and know each other well enough to know when to say it.

And once more the gracious ending: 'just as you are doing.' Paul has now used that phrase three times (4:1, 4:10, and here). He does not correct a fault they do not have. He names what is already true and asks for more of it — which is a harder discipline than criticism, and a good deal more effective.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A rapid series of instructions for the congregation's common life. They are to respect those who labour among them, lead them and admonish them (v.12), esteeming them very highly in love because of their work — and to be at peace among themselves (v.13).

Then three different people needing three different treatments: admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all of them (v.14). Nobody is to repay evil for evil; instead they are to pursue the good of one another and of everyone (v.15).

Three commands follow that have become among the best known Paul wrote: rejoice always (v.16), pray without ceasing (v.17), give thanks in all circumstances — for this is God's will in Christ Jesus for them (v.18). And four about the Spirit's work in the assembly: do not quench the Spirit (v.19), do not despise prophecies (v.20), but test everything and hold fast what is good (v.21), abstaining from every form of evil (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Discernment Instead of Either Extreme

Verses 19-22 give the balance the church has needed ever since. Some at Thessalonica were dismissive of prophetic speech, and one can see why — the second letter has to deal with a claimed message announcing that the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thess 2:2). When people have been misled by something claiming the Spirit's authority, the instinct is to shut the whole thing down.

Paul refuses that instinct and refuses its opposite. The remedy for false prophecy is not the abolition of prophecy but dokimazo — the assayer's word from 2:4, weighing metal to see whether it is genuine. And testing has two outcomes, not one: hold fast what is good, abstain from what is bad. Discernment that only ever rejects has done half its job. A church can be so afraid of disorder that it smothers the fire, and so afraid of smothering the fire that it swallows anything; Paul asks for the harder combination of open and awake.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: This congregation was months old and already had recognised people labouring, leading and admonishing. Paul gives them no title and names none of them — he describes them by their work, and grounds the honour owed them in exactly that: 'because of their work'. The guard that follows is deliberate. Having told them to esteem certain people very highly, he immediately adds 'be at peace among yourselves', because attitudes to leadership are one of the commonest fault lines in any church.

Now: Verse 14 is the most practical sentence about pastoral care in the New Testament, and its force is in the mismatching. Ataktoi is a military word — out of rank — and the idle need telling. Oligopsychoi means small-souled, and the fainthearted need encouraging. The weak need someone to take their arm. Give the wrong response and you do damage: the lazy man comforted stays lazy, the frightened man rebuked despairs, the weak man exhorted falls over. Note that Paul asks this of 'brothers' — of everyone, not only of leaders. And in verse 18, read the preposition: give thanks in all circumstances, not for them. Paul never asks anyone to be grateful for evil.

verseByVerse.quote: We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three descriptions of the same people, and they are not three offices but one job seen from three sides. They labour among you — kopiao, the exhausting word from 1:3, work to the point of weariness. They are over you in the Lord — proistemi, which means to stand in front of, and carries both leading and caring for. And they admonish you — noutheteo, to put in mind, the word for correction that is meant to change someone.

Notice how young this was. This church was months old, and it already had recognised people doing this. Paul does not name them or give them a title; he describes them by their work, which is the only credential on offer here.

What the congregation owes them is two things. 'Respect' — literally to know them, to recognise them for what they are, which implies actually paying attention to who is doing the work. And 'esteem them very highly in love because of their work.' The phrase is emphatic; Paul stacks the intensifiers. But the ground is stated exactly: not because of their office, their gifts or their personality — because of their work.

That cuts in two directions and is meant to. A leader is to be honoured for labouring, which means the honour is tied to something real rather than to status. And a congregation that grasps what the work actually costs — the broken nights, the conversation nobody wants to have, the sermon prepared while the family waits — will find the esteem easier to produce.

'Be at peace among yourselves.' It is the last clause of the paragraph and reads almost as an aside, but its placement is deliberate. Attitudes to leadership are one of the commonest fault lines in a congregation, and Paul has just told them to esteem certain people very highly. He immediately guards it: not so highly that you form parties around them. Peace among the members is the condition in which anyone can lead at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul turns from what the congregation owes its leaders to what its members owe each other — and three different people get three different treatments. That is the whole point of the verse.

Admonish the idle. The word ataktoi is military: out of rank, out of step, the soldier who will not keep formation. It is the same problem as 4:11 — those who had stopped working, very likely because of excitement about the Lord's return. What they need is not sympathy. They need to be told.

Encourage the fainthearted. Oligopsychoi — literally small-souled, the person whose courage has run low. In a church losing members to persecution and burying friends, there would have been plenty. What they need is not admonishing. Tell a frightened person to pull himself together and you have made him worse.

Help the weak. The verb means to hold onto, to cling to, to support — the word for taking someone's arm. Not advice, not exhortation, but bearing some of the weight.

Set the three together and you have the most practical sentence about pastoral care in the New Testament. The same trouble in three people requires three different responses, and giving the wrong one does damage. The lazy man comforted stays lazy; the frightened man rebuked despairs; the weak man exhorted simply falls over. This is the skill of reading the person in front of you rather than dispensing what you find easiest to give — and note that Paul asks it not of pastors but of 'brothers', of everybody.

Then the clause that makes it possible: 'be patient with them all.' Makrothymeo — long-tempered, slow to boil. It covers all three categories, because all three will try you: the idle will not start, the fainthearted will not be reassured, the weak will need holding up again next week. Patience is what keeps you doing the right thing for the eleventh time.

verseByVerse.quote: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'See that no one repays anyone evil for evil.' The phrasing repays attention: not merely 'do not repay evil' but see to it that no one does. The congregation is made responsible for one another's behaviour here. Retaliation is a community problem, not a private one.

And remember who is being told this. These were people under real hostility — driven from families, squeezed out of trades, watching their teacher run out of town. They had genuine grievances against identifiable neighbours. This is not an abstract ethic offered to the comfortable.

Then Paul goes past the prohibition, which is where the verse becomes difficult: 'always seek to do good to one another and to everyone.' Not merely refrain from revenge. Pursue the good of the people making your life hard. The verb means to chase after.

This is the teaching of Jesus, and Paul has clearly received it: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27-28). It is one of the marks that the ethics of the earliest churches were not invented by them but handed down.

In honesty this is among the hardest commands in Scripture, and it helps to see what makes it possible rather than merely admirable. Two things stand behind it in this letter. The Lord is an avenger (4:6) — so the wronged Christian is not required to secure justice himself, because Someone else has undertaken to. And these people are not destined for wrath (5:9) — they have received the exact treatment they are now being asked to extend. Refusing revenge is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It is handing it to a court that will actually deal with it, and treating your neighbour the way you were treated when you deserved otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three commands, five words in Greek, and they are among the best-known lines Paul ever wrote. They are also, on first reading, impossible. Take them one at a time.

'Rejoice always.' Not: be cheerful about everything. This is a letter to a grieving, persecuted church, and Paul is not asking them to pretend. Joy here is what it was in 1:6 — joy given by the Holy Spirit in the middle of much affliction. It is possible always because its ground is outside the circumstances, and that is the only reason it can be commanded at all.

'Pray without ceasing.' The word does not mean uninterrupted. It was used of a persistent cough — something that keeps recurring, that never fully goes away. Paul is not requiring perpetual formal prayer, which would make ordinary work impossible. He is describing a life in which the line to God is never actually closed: the running commentary of a heart that keeps turning to him through the day.

'Give thanks in all circumstances.' Read the preposition carefully, because it matters enormously to a suffering reader. In all circumstances, not for all circumstances. Paul does not ask anyone to be grateful for evil, for a death, for a betrayal. He asks for thanksgiving to continue inside such things, because God's goodness does not pause when circumstances turn. Anyone who has sat with a bereaved Christian who could still thank God for something has seen it done.

Then the sentence that binds them: 'for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.' It is the second time the letter has told us plainly what God's will is — the first was sanctification (4:3). Between them they cover the ground. People agonise over discovering God's will as though it were hidden. Two things at least are published: he wants you holy, and he wants you rejoicing, praying and thankful.

And notice that these three are held together for a reason. Joy without prayer becomes shallow optimism; prayer without thanksgiving becomes a list of complaints; thanksgiving without joy becomes a duty. Each keeps the others honest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four short commands about the Spirit's work in the assembly, and they are arranged as two pairs — two prohibitions, then the corrective, then the outcome.

'Do not quench the Spirit.' The verb is used of putting out a fire, and the metaphor is deliberate: the Spirit is spoken of as flame. You do not extinguish a fire by attacking it; you do it by smothering it, or by simply not feeding it. Paul does not say how it happens here, and the next line suggests one way.

'Do not despise prophecies.' Evidently some in Thessalonica were dismissive of prophetic speech in the meeting. Given what the next chapter of their story looks like — the second letter has to deal with a claimed message saying the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thess 2:2) — one can see why. When people have been misled by something claiming the Spirit's authority, the instinct is to shut the whole thing down.

Paul refuses that instinct, and his answer is the balance the church has needed ever since: 'but test everything.' Not credulity, which accepts whatever is confidently asserted. Not cynicism, which rejects everything to be safe. Testing — dokimazo, the assayer's word from 2:4, weighing metal to see whether it is genuine. The remedy for false prophecy is not the abolition of prophecy but discernment.

And testing has two results, one in each direction. 'Hold fast what is good' — grip it, keep it. Discernment that only ever rejects has failed at half its job. 'Abstain from every form of evil' — and the word for form means appearance or kind. Whatever the testing shows to be bad, drop it entirely, whatever authority was claimed for it.

What holds the four together is that they refuse both of the easy positions. A church can be so afraid of disorder that it quenches the Spirit, and so afraid of quenching the Spirit that it swallows anything. Paul asks for the harder combination: open, and awake. That takes more work than either extreme, which is presumably why so few congregations manage it.

verseByVerse.ref: 5:23–28 – Kept Blameless, and the Last Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter closes in prayer. May the God of peace himself sanctify them completely, and keep their whole spirit and soul and body blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus (v.23) — and then the prayer turns into a promise: he who calls them is faithful, and he will do it (v.24).

Three final requests: pray for us (v.25); greet all the brothers with a holy kiss (v.26); and, under oath before the Lord, have this letter read to all of them (v.27). Then the last word, which is the first word: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you (v.28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Whole Persons, and Who Does the Keeping

'Spirit and soul and body' raises an old question — is a human being made of three parts or two? Some have read it as trichotomy, taking spirit as the God-ward faculty, soul as the conscious self and body as the physical frame. The historic Reformed reading, from Calvin onward, is dichotomy: spirit and soul name the one immaterial dimension of human nature from two angles, not two separate compartments. Paul uses the terms interchangeably elsewhere (1 Cor 2:11; 15:45), and the construction matches Deuteronomy 6:5 — heart, soul and strength — which nobody reads as an anatomy. It is a way of saying the whole of you, and that is the point: no part of a life left unsanctified.

Two grammatical details carry the comfort. 'Be kept' is passive — they are not keeping themselves, they are being kept, and the difference between those two sentences is the difference between exhaustion and rest. And 'he who calls you' is present tense, as in 2:12: God is calling them still. Paul has asked for something enormous and then declares it as good as done, on the ground not of their staying power but of the caller's faithfulness — the same confidence as Philippians 1:6.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath in verse 27 is startling, and it is the only place Paul does anything like it. The reason is almost certainly the word all. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church, and most believers met Scripture with their ears; Paul wants nobody left out — not the illiterate, not the slaves who might miss a meeting, not the fainthearted and the weak he has just named. He has written things here that grieving and frightened people need, and he will not have it circulate among a few. It is also a quiet indication of how these documents were regarded from the start: nobody puts a congregation under oath about private correspondence.

Now: The holy kiss (v.26) looks quaint until you notice its range — all the brothers. In a room holding slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, the wealthy householder and the day labourer, that instruction dismantles something. You cannot greet a man as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you. And note the small change in the closing grace: the letter opened 'grace to you', grace arriving; it ends 'grace be with you', grace staying. Paul could not come himself — Satan had blocked the road and Timothy went in his place. What he could send was this.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter turns to prayer, and Paul asks for the one thing that has run through it from the beginning: 'may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely.'

'The God of peace himself' — not an angel, not a principle, not a programme. And the emphasis answers everything the letter has asked of them. Paul has told them to be holy, to work, to love, to stay awake, to be patient, to test everything. Now he prays, because he knows perfectly well that nobody produces this by effort.

'Completely' is holoteleis, a compound of whole and end — entirely, right through to the finish. Then he says it again in another way: 'may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless.' Nothing is left outside.

That threefold phrase raises an old question: is a person made of three parts or two? Some have read it as trichotomy — spirit as the God-ward faculty, soul as the conscious self, body as the physical frame, three compartments. The historic Reformed reading, from Calvin on, is dichotomy: spirit and soul name the one immaterial dimension of human nature from two angles, not two separate parts. Paul himself uses the words interchangeably (cf. 1 Cor 2:11; 15:45), and the pattern is familiar from Deuteronomy 6:5 — love the LORD with all your heart and soul and strength — which nobody takes as an anatomy. It is a way of saying the whole of you. And that is the point here: Paul is not sketching the structure of the soul; he is praying that no part of a life be left unsanctified.

Note also that 'be kept' is passive. They are not keeping themselves. Someone is keeping them, and the difference between those two sentences is the difference between exhaustion and rest.

Then verse 24, and the prayer becomes a promise: 'He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.' The calling is present tense again, as in 2:12 — he goes on calling. And the guarantee is not their staying power but his character. Paul has just asked God for something enormous, and then tells them it is as good as done, because the one being asked does not begin what he will not finish.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three requests, and each is more revealing than it looks.

'Brothers, pray for us.' Three words, no elaboration. The apostle who has prayed for them constantly (1:2), night and day (3:10), asks them to pray for him. He has just finished praying that God would sanctify them completely — and then asks for their prayers in return, without any suggestion that the traffic runs one way. It is the same instinct as 3:7, where their faith comforted him.

'Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.' The kiss on the cheek was an ordinary greeting in that world, between family and close friends. What is not ordinary is the range Paul gives it: all the brothers. In a room containing slaves and masters, Jews and Greeks, men and women, the wealthy householder and the day labourer, that instruction dismantles something. You cannot greet a man as family every week and go on regarding him as beneath you. The adjective 'holy' distinguishes it from the ordinary social kiss: this one is set apart, and it means what it says.

Then the third, and the tone shifts sharply: 'I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.' The verb is strong — to adjure, to place someone under solemn obligation. It is the only time Paul does anything like this, and it is unexpected in a letter with so little friction in it.

Why so forceful? Almost certainly because of that word all again. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church; most believers met Scripture with their ears. Paul wants nobody left out — not the illiterate, not the slaves who might not be at every meeting, not the fainthearted and the weak he has just named. He has written things in this letter that grieving and frightened people need, and he will not have it circulate among a few.

There is also a quiet indication here of how these documents were regarded from the start. Paul expects his letter to be read to the whole assembly, under oath, as a matter of obligation. That is not how anyone treats private correspondence.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.'

The letter opened with grace (1:1) and closes with it, and the two form a frame around everything between. That is not a formality; it is a statement about what the whole thing is made of. Inside the frame stand a young church under persecution, a congregation burying its dead, a man defending himself against slander, and a list of commands most of us find hard. All of it sits inside grace.

Notice the small change from the greeting. There Paul wrote 'grace to you' — grace arriving. Here it is 'grace be with you' — grace staying, accompanying them into whatever came next. He could not come himself; Satan had blocked the road and Timothy had gone in his place. What he can send is this.

And what came next was not easy. They would go on being a small, pressured minority in a proud Roman city. Paul would write a second letter within months because the confusion about the Lord's coming had got worse rather than better. Every one of them would eventually be among those who had fallen asleep. The last word he gives them is the thing that would still be true through all of it.

So the earliest surviving Christian letter ends where it began, and where every one of Paul's letters ends. Not with an exhortation, not with a warning, not with a summary of the argument — but with grace, handed over as the one provision that does not run out.
